py_basics.summary: Python programs are built from values (numbers, text, booleans), variables that name them, and control flow (if, for, while) that decides what runs. `/` always gives a float; `//` divides and rounds down.
key_points: Variables point at values; types are checked at run time
py_basics.analogy: A variable is a label stuck on a box; the box holds the value.

py_functions.summary: A function packages steps behind a name. It returns a value only if it executes `return`; otherwise it returns None. Default arguments are evaluated once, so a mutable default (like a list) is shared between calls.
key_points: Avoid mutable defaults; use None and create inside
py_functions.analogy: A function is a recipe: ingredients in, dish out.
py_functions.pitfall: Forgetting `return`, or using `bucket=[]` as a default.

py_collections.summary: Lists keep order and allow duplicates, dicts map keys to values with fast lookup, and sets keep unique items. Choose by the question you need to answer: order, lookup, or uniqueness.
py_collections.analogy: A dict is a phone book: you look up by name, not by position.
py_collections.pitfall: Searching a list repeatedly when a dict would do.

git_basics.summary: Git records snapshots. You edit files, stage the changes with `git add`, save them with `git commit`, and share them with `git push`.
git_basics.analogy: Staging is putting items in a box; commit seals and labels it; push ships it.

linux_cli.summary: The command line lets you navigate (cd, ls, pwd), manage files (mkdir, cp, rm) and combine commands with pipes (|), where the output of one command becomes the input of the next.
key_points: Paths can be absolute or relative
linux_cli.analogy: A pipe is a conveyor belt between machines.

sql_relational_model.summary: A relational database stores data in tables of rows and columns. A primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key in another table points to it and links the two tables.
sql_relational_model.summary_hi: Relational database data ko tables (rows aur columns) mein rakhta hai. Primary key har row ko unique pehchaan deti hai; foreign key doosre table ki row ko point karke dono tables ko jodti hai.
key_points: Primary key = unique id of a row
Foreign key = pointer to another table's key
sql_relational_model.analogy: Customers and orders are like a class register and its homework slips: each slip carries the roll number of the student it belongs to.
sql_relational_model.pitfall: Repeating customer details on every order row.

sql_select.summary: SELECT chooses which columns to show and can calculate new values per row; FROM names the table; AS renames a result column. SELECT never changes stored data.
sql_select.summary_hi: SELECT batata hai kaun se columns dikhane hain aur har row par calculation bhi kar sakta hai; FROM table ka naam deta hai; AS result column ko naam deta hai. SELECT stored data ko kabhi nahi badalta.
key_points: List only the columns you need
Expressions like price * 1.18 are computed per row
AS gives a name to the result column
sql_select.analogy: SELECT is choosing which columns of a spreadsheet to look at.
sql_select.example: SELECT name, price * 1.18 AS price_with_gst FROM products

sql_filtering.summary: WHERE keeps only the rows for which the condition is TRUE. AND is evaluated before OR, so use brackets when you mix them. LIKE with % matches patterns; without % it must match the whole value.
sql_filtering.summary_hi: WHERE sirf wahi rows rakhta hai jinke liye condition TRUE ho. AND, OR se pehle evaluate hota hai, isliye dono mix karte waqt brackets lagayein. LIKE ke saath % lagana zaroori hai, warna poori value match honi chahiye.
sql_filtering.analogy: WHERE is a sieve: only rows passing every test fall through.
sql_filtering.pitfall: city='A' OR city='B' AND date>... without brackets.
sql_filtering.example: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE (city = 'Lucknow' OR city = 'Varanasi') AND signup_date > '2025-03-01'

sql_null.summary: NULL means 'unknown', not zero or empty text. Any comparison with NULL (even NULL = NULL) is UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, and decide explicitly what to do with NULL rows when you use <>.
sql_null.summary_hi: NULL ka matlab 'pata nahi' hai — na zero, na khaali text. NULL ke saath har comparison (NULL = NULL bhi) UNKNOWN hota hai aur WHERE sirf TRUE rows rakhta hai. IS NULL / IS NOT NULL use karein.
sql_null.analogy: NULL is a blank answer on an exam sheet: you cannot say it equals or differs from the right answer.
sql_null.pitfall: WHERE status <> 'delivered' silently excludes rows with no status.
sql_null.example: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status <> 'delivered' OR status IS NULL

sql_sorting_limit.summary: Without ORDER BY the order of rows is not defined, so LIMIT alone returns arbitrary rows. ORDER BY ... DESC LIMIT n gives the top n. DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows across all selected columns.
sql_sorting_limit.summary_hi: ORDER BY ke bina rows ka order tay nahi hota, isliye sirf LIMIT arbitrary rows deta hai. Top n ke liye ORDER BY ... DESC LIMIT n use karein. DISTINCT chune hue saare columns ke combination par duplicate hatata hai.
key_points: DISTINCT works on the whole row
Add a tie-breaker column for stable order
sql_sorting_limit.analogy: LIMIT without ORDER BY is grabbing a handful of cards from an unsorted pile.
sql_sorting_limit.example: SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 3

sql_aggregates.summary: Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) turn many rows into one value. They ignore NULLs, except COUNT(*), which counts rows. AVG of 10, 20, NULL is 15.
sql_aggregates.summary_hi: Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) kai rows ko ek value mein badal dete hain. Ye NULL ko ignore karte hain, sirf COUNT(*) rows ginta hai.
key_points: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs
Use COALESCE(x, 0) if NULL should count as 0
sql_aggregates.analogy: An aggregate is a tally sheet that skips blank entries.
sql_aggregates.example: SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_orders, COUNT(status) AS with_status FROM orders

sql_group_by.summary: GROUP BY splits rows into groups by the listed columns, and each aggregate is calculated per group, giving one output row per group. Every non-aggregated column in SELECT must be in GROUP BY. Without GROUP BY an aggregate collapses the whole table to one row.
sql_group_by.summary_hi: GROUP BY rows ko columns ke hisaab se groups mein baantta hai aur har group par aggregate nikalta hai — har group ke liye ek output row. SELECT ka har non-aggregated column GROUP BY mein hona chahiye.
sql_group_by.analogy: Sorting students into classrooms, then counting each classroom.
sql_group_by.pitfall: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) with no GROUP BY.
sql_group_by.example: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id

sql_having.summary: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters whole groups after aggregation. Only HAVING can test COUNT(*) or SUM(...). Logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY.
sql_having.summary_hi: WHERE grouping se pehle individual rows filter karta hai; HAVING aggregation ke baad poore groups filter karta hai. COUNT(*) ya SUM(...) ko sirf HAVING test kar sakta hai.
key_points: Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE
sql_having.analogy: WHERE checks each student at the gate; HAVING checks each class after it formed.
sql_having.example: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1

sql_inner_join.summary: JOIN ... ON combines rows from two tables where the ON condition is true. INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match on both sides. Forgetting the ON condition pairs every row with every row (a cartesian product).
sql_inner_join.summary_hi: JOIN ... ON do tables ki rows ko tab jodta hai jab ON condition true ho. INNER JOIN sirf wahi rows rakhta hai jo dono taraf match karti hain. ON condition bhoolne par har row har row se jud jaati hai.
key_points: Match foreign key to primary key
No ON = cartesian product (12 x 8 = 96 rows)
sql_inner_join.analogy: Matching each homework slip with the student whose roll number is written on it.
sql_inner_join.pitfall: FROM orders, customers with no condition.
sql_inner_join.example: SELECT o.id, c.name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id

sql_outer_join.summary: A LEFT JOIN keeps EVERY row of the left table. Where there is no match, the right-hand columns are NULL. Filtering the right table in WHERE removes those NULL rows and silently turns it into an inner join - put the condition in ON instead. After a LEFT JOIN, count a right-table column (COUNT(o.id)) to get 0 for unmatched rows.
sql_outer_join.summary_hi: LEFT JOIN left table ki HAR row rakhta hai. Jahan match nahi milta, right ke columns NULL ho jaate hain. Right table par WHERE filter lagane se NULL rows hat jaati hain aur wo inner join jaisa ban jaata hai — condition ON mein likhein.
key_points: LEFT JOIN never has fewer rows than the left table
Condition on the right table belongs in ON
sql_outer_join.analogy: A class register: every student is listed, even those who submitted no homework (blank).
sql_outer_join.pitfall: WHERE o.status = 'delivered' cancels the LEFT JOIN.
sql_outer_join.example: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id

sql_multi_table.summary: Joining several tables chains the relationships: each one-to-many join can repeat rows. Sums computed after such a join count a value once per repeat. Count rows after each join, use DISTINCT only when you understand the repeats, and aggregate at the right level.
sql_multi_table.summary_hi: Kai tables join karne par har one-to-many join rows ko repeat kar sakta hai. Aise join ke baad SUM nikalne par value repeat ke hisaab se kai baar gini jaati hai. Har join ke baad rows ginein.
key_points: One-to-many joins repeat the one-side row
sql_multi_table.analogy: If an order has 2 items and you list one line per item, the order total appears on both lines.
sql_multi_table.example: SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) AS total FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.name

sql_subqueries.summary: A subquery is a query inside another query. Use one when you need a computed value (like an average) in a condition. NOT IN misbehaves if the subquery returns NULL; NOT EXISTS is safer.
sql_subqueries.summary_hi: Subquery ek query ke andar doosri query hoti hai. Jab condition mein computed value (jaise average) chahiye tab ise use karein. Subquery NULL de to NOT IN galat result deta hai; NOT EXISTS safe hai.
key_points: Aggregates go in a subquery, not WHERE
sql_subqueries.analogy: Answering 'who is above average?' first needs a separate calculation of the average.
sql_subqueries.example: SELECT name FROM products WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products)

sql_case_expr.summary: CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END computes a value per row based on conditions. Without ELSE, unmatched rows get NULL. It does not change stored data.
sql_case_expr.analogy: A traffic-light rule applied to each row.
sql_case_expr.example: SELECT id, CASE WHEN amount >= 500 THEN 'big' ELSE 'small' END AS size FROM orders

sql_dml.summary: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes existing rows, DELETE removes them. UPDATE and DELETE without a WHERE affect every row, so check the WHERE first (try it as a SELECT).
key_points: DROP removes whole tables, DELETE removes rows
sql_dml.analogy: UPDATE without WHERE is like re-labelling every box in the warehouse.

sql_normalization.summary: Normalisation means storing each fact once and linking tables with keys, so data cannot become inconsistent. Many-to-many relationships need a junction table.
key_points: Avoid repeating customer data on every order
sql_normalization.analogy: Keep one address book and refer to it, instead of rewriting addresses on every letter.

sql_indexes.summary: An index is an extra structure that makes lookups on a column fast, like a book's index. It speeds up reads that filter, join or sort on that column but slows down inserts and updates and uses space.
key_points: Index columns used in WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY of slow queries
sql_indexes.analogy: The index at the back of a textbook: fast lookup, but must be updated when the book changes.

sql_transactions.summary: A transaction groups statements so they succeed or fail together (atomicity). ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Changes are private to your session until COMMIT.
key_points: Isolation: others do not see uncommitted changes
sql_transactions.analogy: A bank transfer: debit and credit must both happen or neither.
sql_transactions.pitfall: Assuming others see your uncommitted changes.

http_basics.summary: HTTP is request/response: a client sends a method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and a URL, the server replies with a status code and a body. GET is read-only. 2xx = success, 4xx = client error (401 not authenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found), 5xx = server error.
key_points: 401 = who are you? 403 = you may not
http_basics.analogy: Ordering at a counter: you make a request, the counter replies with an outcome.
http_basics.pitfall: Using GET links to delete data; mixing up 401 and 403.

rest_apis.summary: REST models things as resources with URLs (nouns) and uses HTTP methods as the actions: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces (idempotent), PATCH updates part, DELETE removes. Status codes tell the result.
key_points: Nouns in URLs, verbs as methods
PUT is idempotent; POST is not
rest_apis.analogy: A library: books have shelf addresses (URLs); borrowing, returning and adding are the actions.

api_auth.summary: Authentication proves who the caller is (for example with a signed JWT or an API key); authorisation decides what they may do. Secrets live on the server, never in front-end code or public repositories.
api_auth.analogy: A wristband at an event proves you entered; zones on it decide where you may go.
api_auth.pitfall: Shipping API keys in browser code.

fastapi_basics.summary: FastAPI maps Python functions to endpoints using decorators like @app.get('/hello'). Type hints and Pydantic models validate input automatically (bad input gets a 422 response) and generate interactive docs.
fastapi_basics.analogy: Each function is a counter at a service desk; the decorator is the sign above it.
fastapi_basics.pitfall: Forgetting type hints, so validation is skipped.

py_db_access.summary: From Python you connect, execute SQL, and commit. Always pass values as parameters (`?` or `%s`) instead of formatting strings, to prevent SQL injection. Changes are visible to others only after commit.
py_db_access.analogy: A parameter is a sealed envelope: its contents can never rewrite the letter's instructions.

docker_basics.summary: A Docker image is a packaged template (code plus dependencies); a container is a running instance of an image. Containers share the host kernel, so they start fast and are lighter than virtual machines.
docker_basics.analogy: A shipping container: same box runs the same on any ship.
docker_basics.pitfall: Thinking a container is a full VM.

comm_self_intro.summary: A professional 60 to 90-second self-introduction sets the tone for an interview. It covers who you are and current studies/work, your technical focus and primary project, and why you are excited about this specific role.
comm_self_intro.summary_hi: Ek peshewar 60 se 90 second ka parichay interview ka sur tay karta hai. Isme aap kaun hain, aapka technical focus aur mukhya project, tatha is role mein ruchi shamil hoti hai.
comm_self_intro.analogy: A movie trailer: gives the highlights that make the interviewer want to know more.
comm_self_intro.pitfall: Reciting your entire CV line-by-line chronologically.

comm_star_story.summary: The STAR framework structures behavioural answers: Situation (context), Task (your objective), Action (what YOU specifically did, using 'I'), Result (measurable outcome), and Reflection (what you learned).
comm_star_story.summary_hi: STAR framework vyavahar-aadhrit uttar ko structure karta hai: Situation (context), Task (aapka lakshya), Action (aapne akele kya kiya, 'I' use karein), Result (thos parinaam), aur Reflection (kya seekha).
comm_star_story.analogy: A case report: setting, diagnostic challenge, treatment given, and patient outcome.
comm_star_story.pitfall: Spending 80% of the time on the situation and forgetting the result or your own actions.

comm_project_walkthrough.summary: Explaining a technical project requires presenting the problem statement, high-level architecture, your personal ownership, key technical trade-offs, and how you solved a challenging bug or bottleneck.
comm_project_walkthrough.summary_hi: Project samjhate waqt problem statement, architecture, apna personal yogdaan, technical trade-offs aur mushkil bug solve karne ka tarika batayein.
key_points: State the architecture and data flow
Articulate why technology choices were made over alternatives
comm_project_walkthrough.analogy: A building blueprint walkthrough: the overall structure plus the specific load-bearing walls you engineered.
comm_project_walkthrough.pitfall: Describing UI features without explaining architecture, trade-offs, or personal responsibilities.
